strengths: Soundness: The method is technically plausible and clearly specified: Grounding DINO proposes category instances, DINOv2 matches them to five reference views, SAM2 segments/tracks the selected instance, and a tint-aligned instruction rewrite conditions a frozen VLA. Large gains are reported consistently across Google Robot, WidowX, Franka, and SO-101 settings—for example, pen-holder CMR improves from 10.5% to 89.2%, and average real-world pointing success from 30.0% to 80.0%.

Significance: Personalized instance-level manipulation is practically important and insufficiently measured by conventional category-level VLA evaluations. The two adapted simulation benchmarks and 160-trial physical-robot study provide useful initial testbeds spanning selection and pick-and-place tasks.

Evaluation breadth is unusually good for a simple inference-time method: the paper covers two VLA variants, four robot embodiments, single- and multi-camera observations, multiple object categories, simulation perturbations, physical experiments, runtime, and failure analysis.

Presentation: The central problem, pipeline, and empirical conclusions are easy to understand. Figures and tables are legible, and the appendix gives useful training, prompt, token-baseline, qualitative-rollout, and error-taxonomy details.

The authors appropriately acknowledge substantive limitations, including dependence on upstream grounding, cross-view inconsistency, short-horizon tabletop tasks, and underlying manipulation competence. The discussion also recognizes privacy, user control, revocation, and safety issues associated with storing personal references.
weaknesses: Soundness: The experiments do not isolate which component causes the improvement. There are no ablations for mask highlighting versus instruction rewriting, tint color/opacity, tracking, number of references, encoder choice, or per-view processing, nor comparisons with oracle masks. Because VAP receives an explicit target localization from a strong detector/retriever/segmenter while the main competitors receive only language or a learned token, the results establish the value of this full perception-assisted pipeline but not the claimed mechanism of visual attentive prompting specifically.

The personalization diversity is limited. Each task/category appears to use one designated personal instance with two fixed distractors, so many reported episodes are perturbations or repeated rollouts of a small set of identities. The paper does not test many independently sampled users/targets per category, new distractor sets, reference-image quality, or cases where target and distractors are nearly identical. This weakens claims of broad personalization generalization.

Statistical reporting is inadequate. Results are point estimates without confidence intervals, variance, or significance tests, including the physical study with only 20 trials per task. It is also unclear whether repeated simulation runs use independent stochastic seeds.

The episode accounting is inconsistent: Personalized-VLABench is described as 50 episodes per task and 250 total in Section 4/Table 1, Table 4 says 10 runs of 25 episodes per task, and Appendix Table 9 reports 125×10 episodes. Bridge is similarly summarized as 96 episodes in Table 1 but evaluated as 96×10 elsewhere. These discrepancies obstruct interpretation and reproducibility.

Originality is moderate rather than high. The implementation composes established open-vocabulary detection, embedding retrieval, segmentation/tracking, visual highlighting, and template rewriting. The novel value lies mainly in the problem formulation, integration, and benchmark construction; stronger comparisons to alternative reference-conditioned segmentation/retrieval and visual-prompting pipelines are needed.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite substantial appendix detail. The manuscript does not provide a code/data release statement, exact model checkpoints and software versions, detector thresholds, segmentation settings, tint opacity/color policy, complete success predicates, environment randomization details, asset identifiers/licenses, or physical evaluation protocol. Appendix A.3 also appears to swap the headings of the short- and long-description prompts.

The soft-prompt baseline is an imperfect proxy: it is trained in a VLM recognition task and copied into the VLA rather than optimized for action prediction. Its use of test-time distractors as hard negatives is favorable but also departs from a realistic deployment protocol. Consequently, outperforming it does not decisively establish superiority over well-designed learned personalization approaches.

The limitations discussion is honest, but ethical treatment remains prospective. Personal-object images can reveal sensitive possessions and environments, yet the implemented system provides no stated storage duration, access controls, deletion/revocation mechanism, consent protocol, or privacy evaluation; physical-robot safety procedures are also unspecified.

strengths: Soundness: The paper identifies a practical instance-level personalization problem and presents a coherent training-free pipeline combining open-vocabulary detection, DINOv2 matching, SAM2 segmentation/tracking, visual highlighting, and instruction rewriting. Significance: Manipulating a user-designated object among same-category distractors is useful and insufficiently captured by standard VLA evaluations. The proposed simulation adaptations and physical setup provide a potentially useful starting point for studying this problem.

Presentation: The method and motivation are generally easy to follow, with helpful pipeline figures, per-task results, runtime measurements, qualitative rollouts, and an unusually informative failure taxonomy distinguishing grounding, cross-view, and downstream-control errors.

The evaluation includes several embodiments and both simulation and physical experiments. Reporting Correct Movement Ratio alongside task success usefully separates correct-object interaction from complete manipulation.
The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges reliance on external perception, cross-view inconsistency, short-horizon tabletop tasks, and the need to protect personal reference data.
weaknesses: Soundness: The experiments do not isolate which part of VAP produces the gains. There are no ablations for detector/retriever quality, tracking, mask versus box prompts, tint color or opacity, instruction rewriting, number and diversity of reference images, or oracle masks. Consequently, the evidence supports the full engineered pipeline but provides little scientific understanding of its mechanism or bottlenecks.

The comparison set is inadequate for the central claim. Despite discussing RoboGround, MOKA, PIVOT, TraceVLA, and related grounded visual prompting methods, the experiments compare only against an unmodified VLA and text/token prompting. A baseline that localizes the reference object and communicates a box, point, crop, or mask through an established visual-prompting approach is essential; otherwise the results mostly establish that explicitly highlighting the target beats asking a frozen VLA to infer its identity from text.

The benchmark has limited identity diversity: it appears to use only one designated personal target per category, with two distractors, across six Personalized-SIMPLER tasks, five selection categories, and eight real-world categories. This does not convincingly establish generalization across users, many target identities within a category, larger distractor sets, novel backgrounds, or naturally changing personal objects. Personalized-VLABench is reduced to touching an object rather than the benchmark's more substantive manipulation or reasoning tasks.

Statistical reporting is insufficient. The paper gives percentages without confidence intervals, variance, or significance tests, even for real-world tasks with only 20 trials per task. It also does not clearly specify placement randomization, trial independence, success adjudication, or whether baseline trials used identical configurations. Some episode counts are internally confusing: Table 1 lists 96 Bridge and 250 VLABench episodes, whereas Tables 3 and 4 describe ten runs of 24 or 25 episodes per task, and Appendix Table 9 uses still different aggregate notation.

Originality is modest. VAP is primarily a composition of existing detector, embedding-retrieval, segmentation/tracking, and mark-based visual-prompting components. The personalized-object formulation is useful, but the paper does not contribute a new learning method, grounding algorithm, or substantive analysis showing why its particular design is preferable to simpler grounded prompting.

Reproducibility is currently weak. The manuscript gives backbone training steps and component names but omits important implementation details such as model variants, detection thresholds, crop preprocessing, vote tie-breaking, segmentation/tracker settings, tint parameters, control frequency, reference-image acquisition, random seeds, and detailed evaluation protocols. No code, benchmark release, data availability statement, or complete list and licensing information for simulation assets is provided.

Presentation contains avoidable inconsistencies. Appendix A.3 appears to reverse the short- and long-description prompt labels, Table 7's caption says both descriptions are used as rich prompts, and the main text alternates between pointing and selection terminology. The paper also repeatedly characterizes performance as robust despite VAP failing 31.9-38.4% of episodes in several settings and multi-view inconsistency causing roughly half or more of failures there.

Ethics and privacy are mentioned only prospectively. Because the method stores reference images of personal possessions, a deployable account should specify retention, revocation, access control, and whether processing is actually local. This is not a fatal issue for the present experiments, which involve no reported human-subject study, but it matters to the paper's home-assistance framing.

strengths: Soundness: The core idea is plausible and supported by consistently large gains across two simulation suites and a physical SO-101 robot. For example, VAP raises success from 8.5% to 60.3% on the SIMPLER pen-holder task and improves average real-world pointing success from 30.0% to 80.0%.

Significance: Personal-object manipulation is a useful and underexplored VLA capability. The reference-image formulation is practical, and the evaluation spans multiple embodiments, camera configurations, object categories, and both selection and pick-and-place tasks.

Originality: The individual components—Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2, visual highlighting, and instruction rewriting—are established, but their integration as a training-free personalization adapter for closed-loop VLA control offers a useful new task framing and empirical contribution.
Presentation: The method and motivation are generally clear, with effective diagrams, readable tables, component runtime measurements, and extensive qualitative rollouts.

The baseline suite includes generic VLAs, short and detailed language descriptions, and learned concept tokens. The appendix makes a serious effort to strengthen and analyze the token-learning baseline, including recognition accuracy, embedding-space comparisons, and attention visualizations.

The paper discusses limitations honestly and quantifies failure modes. In particular, it identifies cross-view inconsistency as 59.2% and 50.9% of failures in the multi-view simulation and real-world settings, respectively, rather than concealing this weakness.
weaknesses: Soundness: The experiments do not isolate which part of VAP causes the gains. There are no ablations for instance retrieval, segmentation, temporal tracking, tint overlay, or instruction rewriting, and no oracle-mask condition. Consequently, the evidence supports the full pipeline but not the paper's more specific attribution to visual attentive prompting.

The comparison set lacks simple perception-matched alternatives, such as using the same retrieved box with cropping, a bounding-box marker, mask-only prompting, or an oracle/retrieval-only controller. It also lacks a baseline that directly conditions on reference images where the backbone permits this. Thus, the results do not establish that the proposed prompt representation is preferable to other ways of exploiting the same strong external grounder.

No confidence intervals, statistical tests, or seed-level variance are reported. This is especially consequential for the physical evaluation, which uses only 20 trials per task, and for several VLABench margins that are only a few percentage points.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Exact Sketchfab assets, scene-generation procedures, reference images, detector thresholds, crop preprocessing, tint color/opacity, tie-breaking in the reference-voting rule, and detailed SAM2 tracking settings are not specified. The manuscript also does not state that code, benchmark assets, or evaluation configurations will be released.

Episode accounting is inconsistent or unclear: Table 1 lists 96 Bridge and 250 VLABench episodes, while the result captions describe 10 runs of 24 episodes per Bridge task and 10 runs of 25 episodes per VLABench task; Appendix Table 9 gives yet another aggregate notation. The hard-prompt appendix also appears to swap the labels of the short and long description-generation prompts.

The scope is narrower than some framing suggests: evaluation covers one designated personal object at a time, mostly uncluttered tabletop scenes, only 13 personal categories, and short-horizon skills. The real-world backbone itself is fine-tuned on 250 task-specific demonstrations, so the accurate claim is training-free per-object personalization, not a wholly training-free deployed system.

The method assumes that the personalized phrase can be reduced to a known generic category and that the target is visible and detectable. Per-view matching always selects a proposal, with no described confidence or abstention mechanism; the reported multi-view failures show that this can produce confidently contradictory prompts.

Originality is moderate because the algorithm is predominantly a straightforward composition of pretrained detection, embedding matching, segmentation/tracking, and an established visual-mark prompting technique. The benchmark framing and breadth of evaluation carry more novelty than the technical mechanism itself.

Research ethics receive limited treatment. Although the discussion briefly mentions privacy and revocation, the paper does not specify storage, retention, consent, or on-device handling of potentially sensitive personal-object images, nor operational safeguards when grounding fails on a physical robot.

strengths: Soundness: The method is technically plausible and well motivated: reference-based detection/matching, mask tracking, and an aligned color-word instruction rewrite form a coherent input-side adapter for frozen VLAs. Large improvements appear consistently across three simulated settings and a physical SO-101 robot, including gains from 8.5% to 60.3% success on the SIMPLER pen-holder task and from 30.0% to 80.0% average success on real-world selection tasks.

Evidence and analysis: The evaluation covers multiple robots, camera configurations, object categories, and task types. Component ablations show that mask highlighting and instruction rewriting are jointly necessary, compare mask and box prompts, vary opacity and reference count, and examine voting versus averaging. The conditional failure taxonomy also usefully separates grounding, cross-view, and downstream-control errors.

Significance: Instance-level personalization is an important practical gap in current VLAs. A method that registers an unseen personal object using roughly five images and requires no per-object VLA optimization could be useful in deployed assistive robotics.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear and visually polished. The pipeline, benchmark construction, qualitative rollouts, runtime breakdown, and limitations are explained accessibly. The discussion candidly identifies cross-view inconsistency and dependence on the underlying manipulation policy.

Originality: Although its components are established, applying coupled visual highlighting and instruction rewriting to personal-object VLA control, together with dedicated simulation and real-world benchmarks, provides a useful system-level contribution.
weaknesses: The central causal evidence is incomplete. VAP delegates instance identification to a strong external stack comprising Grounding DINO, DINOv2, SAM2, and a tracker, then converts the answer into an easy color-conditioned command. Comparisons are primarily against generic, textual, and transferred-token baselines, not against existing grounded robotic visual-prompting systems or simple alternatives such as target cropping, background suppression, pointing markers, coordinates, or oracle grounding. The box ablation helps, but does not establish that the proposed design is preferable to the broader set of natural perception-to-control interfaces.

The evaluation reporting contains material inconsistencies. Table 1 lists 96 Bridge and 250 VLABench episodes; Tables 3 and 4 describe ten runs of 24 episodes per task and ten runs of 50 episodes per task, respectively; Table 9 instead reports 96x10 Bridge episodes and 125x10 VLABench episodes. These conflicting denominators make the experimental protocol and failure percentages difficult to audit.

Uncertainty is inadequately reported. Tables 2–4 provide only means despite repeated runs, without standard deviations, confidence intervals, seeds, or significance tests. Each real-world task has only 20 trials, so estimates occur in coarse five-point increments. The very large gains are encouraging, but smaller cross-method and ablation differences are not convincingly supported.

Reproducibility is below the standard expected for a benchmark paper. There is no code or benchmark release statement, and important details are missing, including exact perception checkpoints and thresholds, SAM2 configuration, proposal filtering, optimizer learning rate and other training parameters, randomization protocols, success criteria, camera specifications, and evaluation seeds. Referring to token learning as using the original method's hyperparameters is also insufficient, although listing the generated textual descriptions is helpful.

External validity is limited. Experiments use only the pi-family of VLAs, tabletop scenes, short-horizon tasks, one target with two same-category distractors, and a small set of curated categories. The reference crops are produced with the same category detector used at test time, and the experiments do not test noisy user photographs, changing illumination/backgrounds, severe occlusion, unknown categories, detector failures, or naturally occurring homes. Thus broad claims about personalizing frozen VLAs should be narrowed.

The contribution is substantially compositional rather than algorithmically novel: open-vocabulary detection, frozen embedding retrieval, segmentation/tracking, visual highlighting, and template rewriting are existing techniques. The benchmark and empirical synthesis are valuable, but positioning the method as inference-time input optimization overstates what is essentially a hand-designed perception-and-prompting pipeline.

The soft-prompt baseline is only an indirect proxy: its token is learned for VLM yes/no recognition and copied into the VLA rather than optimized for action prediction. Its use of deployment distractors as hard negatives is transparently disclosed, but strong VQA accuracy and embedding-space alignment do not establish that this is a competitive control-oriented personalization baseline.

Limitations are discussed honestly, but ethics and privacy receive only a brief future-work remark. A personal-object memory can expose sensitive possessions and ownership relationships; the paper should describe storage, consent, deletion, access control, and any transmission of reference images to external services. Physical safety considerations for erroneous grounding and wrong-object manipulation should also be addressed.

strengths: Soundness: The central mechanism is coherent and testable: reference-based DINOv2 matching, Grounding DINO/SAM2 localization and tracking, and a mask-aligned color cue coupled to an instruction rewrite. End-to-end results show large, consistent gains over the evaluated language and token baselines—for example, 60.3% versus 24.0% success on the SIMPLER pen-holder task and 58.8% versus at most 31.2% average success on real-world pick-and-place tasks.

Experimental breadth and significance: The paper studies a practically relevant instance-level personalization problem across multiple simulated robot settings and a physical SO-101 setup, including selection, picking, and placement. The proposed adapter is computationally lightweight and requires no per-object VLA parameter updates.

Analysis: Component ablations establish that the mask and matched rewrite must be used together, examine reference count, aggregation, prompt geometry, and opacity, and reveal a sensible saturation trend around five reference images. The failure analysis usefully separates grounding, cross-view consistency, and downstream control errors.

Presentation: The paper is generally clear, well illustrated, and unusually candid about important limitations. In particular, it reports that cross-view inconsistency causes 59.2% and 50.9% of failures in the two multi-view settings and explicitly scopes the current system to short-horizon tabletop manipulation.
weaknesses: Soundness: The comparison does not isolate whether VAP is better than strong alternative localized visual interfaces. Most baselines receive only language or a transferred token, whereas VAP receives an explicit target mask produced by a substantial perception stack. Comparisons to existing robotic visual-prompting approaches, crop/background-suppression variants, set-of-mark prompts, and an oracle-mask condition are absent. Consequently, the experiments support this particular pipeline over weakly matched baselines, but not the broader claim that its design is the preferred solution to personalized VLA control.

Generalization is evaluated over very few target identities. The real-world benchmark uses one designated personal instance and two distractors per each of eight categories; the simulation tasks likewise appear to associate each category/task with a fixed personal asset. There is no evaluation that rotates which instance is designated personal, tests many unseen identities per category, or holds out identities and prompt-design choices. This leaves open whether the reported results generalize beyond the small benchmark inventory.

The statistical reporting is inadequate and internally inconsistent. Claims of significant improvement are made without hypothesis tests or confidence intervals. Repeated simulation runs are reported only as means, and the real-world figure's error bars are standard deviations across four heterogeneous tasks rather than uncertainty across trials. More seriously, Personalized-VLABench is described as 250 episodes in Table 1, as 10 runs of 50 episodes per task in Table 4, but as 125×10 episodes in Table 9; these accounts cannot all describe the same evaluation protocol without further explanation.

Originality is modest. The method primarily composes established open-vocabulary detection, foundation-model embeddings, SAM2 tracking, colored-mask visual prompting, and a deterministic text substitution. The new personalization framing and benchmarks are useful, but the technical novelty over prior visual prompting and modular grounding pipelines is limited and is not substantiated through direct empirical comparisons.

The phrase 'training-free' needs tighter qualification. Personal-object registration requires no optimization, but the π0.5 policies are environment-adapted for 60,000 steps using 500 simulated or 250 real teleoperated episodes. Thus the approach is training-free only with respect to each newly registered object, not a training-free route for deploying a generic frozen VLA in a new environment.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a benchmark/method contribution. No code or benchmark release is identified, and essential details are missing or incomplete: simulator configurations and asset splits, random seeds, proposal thresholds, exact model variants, tracker initialization/reset behavior, reference-capture protocol, success tolerances, failure-mode annotation procedure, learning rate and other optimizer settings, and how prompt color/opacity were selected. The use of the final 60,000-step checkpoint without a stated validation protocol further obscures model selection.

The scope remains narrow: exact 'my X' parsing and a known category are assumed; tasks are short-horizon tabletop interactions; multi-view grounding independently selects identities and accounts for roughly half of real-world failures. These are honestly disclosed limitations, but they substantially reduce the current contribution's reach.

Research ethics are only briefly acknowledged. A system that stores images of personal belongings and acts physically around users should discuss memory retention, access control, consent, deletion, ownership conflicts, and robot safety safeguards. No acute ethical violation is evident, but the treatment is too cursory for the envisioned personalized-assistance deployment.

strengths: Soundness: The central claim is supported by substantial gains over generic, hard-prompt, and soft-prompt baselines across Personalized-SIMPLER, Personalized-VLABench, and eight real-world tasks. Component ablations are particularly useful: mask-only and rewrite-only perform far below their combination, and the paper also studies reference aggregation, reference count, prompt geometry, and opacity.

Significance: Personal-object manipulation is a practical and underexplored limitation of current VLAs. Adapting a frozen policy from only a few reference images, without per-object robot demonstrations or parameter updates, would be useful in deployed assistive robotics.

Originality: The individual ingredients are established models and prompting techniques, but their integration into a reference-grounding, tracking, visual-highlighting, and instruction-rewriting pipeline for personalized closed-loop control is a meaningful new application and formulation.

Presentation: The paper is clear, polished, and unusually thorough. The method is easy to understand, figures and tables are legible, and the appendix includes extensive qualitative rollouts, failure analyses, baseline diagnostics, training details, and practical ablations.

The evaluation spans three robot embodiments, single- and multi-camera settings, simulation and physical hardware, and both selection and manipulation tasks. The real-world study includes 160 trials, while the simulation results cover substantially more episodes.

The authors candidly identify important limitations. In particular, they quantify failures from single-view grounding, cross-view inconsistency, and downstream control, and avoid presenting these limitations as solved.
Runtime measurements indicate that tracking adds only about 0.02 seconds per control step, supporting the practical relevance of the approach.
weaknesses: Generality is narrower than the framing suggests. All evaluated policies belong to the π0/π0.5 family, and several results use environment-specific fine-tuning. Thus, VAP is training-free with respect to each personal object, but the experiments do not establish that arbitrary frozen VLA architectures will exploit the same prompts.

The benchmarks contain relatively few personal target instances—apparently one designated target per category, with 2–5 categories in each simulation setting and eight real-world categories. Broader evaluation across many target/distractor identities, backgrounds, lighting conditions, and naturally collected user references is needed to support robust instance-level personalization claims.

Statistical reporting is weak. Most simulation tables provide means without confidence intervals, dispersion, or significance tests. The real-world evaluation has only 20 trials per task, and its error bars summarize variation across four heterogeneous tasks rather than uncertainty over trials. This makes the reliability of smaller differences difficult to assess.

There are internal ambiguities in evaluation counts: Table 1 reports 250 Personalized-VLABench episodes, Table 4 describes 10 runs of 50 episodes for each task, and Table 9 reports 125×10; analogous base-episode versus repeated-run accounting occurs for WidowX. The exact sampling, seed reuse, and aggregation procedure should be reconciled.

The soft-prompt comparison is informative but not conclusive. It learns a recognition token in a separate VLM and transfers it into the VLA rather than optimizing it for action prediction. High VQA accuracy and embedding-space alignment do not guarantee a strong control baseline, so the evidence mainly supports superiority over this particular proxy implementation.

The evaluation does not include an oracle-mask condition or directly report standalone detector, retrieval, segmentation, and tracking accuracy. Such measurements would separate the attainable benefit of prompting from errors in the modular grounding pipeline and clarify which component limits each benchmark.

Reproducibility is only partial. The manuscript gives hardware, datasets, broad training settings, prompts, and one repository commit, but does not state a code/benchmark release and omits several consequential details such as exact perception-model variants and thresholds, random seeds, reference-capture protocol, and precise success criteria.

The method depends on category extraction, open-vocabulary detection, and a rigid “my X” rewrite. Failure to detect a proposal silently removes personalization, while natural referring expressions, unseen category names, moving distractors, and occlusion are not convincingly evaluated.

Ethical risks are modest but underdeveloped for personalized robotics. The discussion briefly mentions privacy, yet does not address retention and access control for users’ reference memories, ownership misbinding in shared spaces, or safeguards against unsafe wrong-object manipulation.
